I call this stuff 'serious automations' -- where a process/decision tree has tens or hundreds of branches.

I see a lot of fluffy things, which are automating the simplest part of a process, leaving a lot for the humans to deal with. This is the thing that can be cloned a 1,000 times in 2 weeks.

I'll give an example. In the system I mentioned, people are scheduled for paid procedures. The procedure takes 2 days, but often we have no-shows on the 2nd day. This 2nd day can be repurposed for someone who was a no-show before - its already paid for, and every penny counts. So the chatbots chase people who may be able to make the appointment last minute, and decrease the costs to operate. There are multiple people in such pools, so the system needs to decide whom to approach, how much time to wait for a decision, and so on. Its gnarly, hard stuff to do right.

The system I mentioned has about 150 such cases, and previously just building the automation would be too expensive, and maintaining it -- too slow. Its a living organism, with thousands of people using the system every day, and more edge cases emerging constantly. Same is true for e.g. GUI elements, widgets, etc. Write it the first time, have your user verify it, persist it, retrieve it.

And maybe you have a couple of people in your org who work through the process of generating a bespoke app that processes data with a GUI optimized for whatever they're doing, but it's all mediated directly through your vendor. The users run through the process all in the web UI of whatever LLM vendor the org's data is silo'd with, the output is a mix of traditional computation and LLM contexts that anybody can maintain via asking the tool to change itself.

Yes, I still hear software development coworkers who want to replace all our tested, deterministic software with non-deterministic, high latency, much more expensive LLM based systems.

Have the LLMs generate even more deterministic software to solve well defined needs and keep the LLMs for solving higher level problems using the deterministic software's outputs as inputs.

> Why would you have a different "app" to do something when you can just do it all in Claude or Gemini or ChatGPT? We'll be there soon enough.

At least from the engineering perspective, the app has a massive advantage: determinism. If I write something in Python or Java or whatever, it has set inputs and outputs and those can be proven to accomplish a computational task because they are working in a logical system.

If I ask an LLM to do that same task, it has inputs and outputs, but the logic isn't anywhere nearly as defined. There will be a chance, no matter how small, that will not act in a way that makes any sort of logical sense given the constraints of the task it was meant to accomplish.

When you combine that with the fact that deterministic applications are far cheaper to run, at least for the foreseeable future, the app wins.

>if the frontier models are so good, why even sell them as your primary money maker?

First, none of these companies are really claiming that their models are so good that this would be a reasonable expectation. They do claim their models can support work across a lot of different industries and roles in order to make that work more efficient, but that's not the same as being a completely autonomous, end-to-end solution.

These companies do basically claim that, at some point, the "end-to-end" version of their models will exist. But until then, they need to survive long enough to be able to actually build such models.

>Couldn't OpenAI or Anthropic make a lot more money by just starting companies themselves that leverage the models and building their own products?

OpenAI and Anthropic are really good at operating AI services. They're likely not good at manufacturing shoes and serving burgers. Again, maybe one day their models will be so good that this won't be a factor, but for now, they need to really focus on what they're good at, otherwise they may be beaten by their competition and they won't exist long enough to create such models.

See: Competitive Advantage

On the same note, it's important to understand that everyone, including AI companies, deal with various capacity constraints. They don't have infinite compute, let alone infinite human attention to keep track of the necessary human-side of any of these businesses. So they're actually dealing with very finite and valuable resources. So would they rather expend those resources trying to build businesses with much more competition and much worse margins? Or focus all of their resources on being the best AI company which they believe will yield the best return on their investment? Again, maybe one day they'll have an AI, blah blah blah

See: Marginal Advantage

>Is selling tokens really the best strategy?

This is a, frankly, obtuse over simplification of what they're doing. Yes, they're selling tokens, but that's like saying all Nvidia does is sell computer parts. Sure, it's (somewhat) accurate, but it completely neglects the very valuable assets that these companies have: their IP.

OpenAI and Anthropic are valuable not because they run inference services; they're valuable because they're actively building SOTA AI services that are becoming increasing advanced. Those models are expected to be incorporated in a lot of different businesses, governments, and even individual's lives. So yes, they're just selling tokens on a technical level, but they're building very tight integrations which they expect will be so valuable to their consumers that they'll continue selling a lot of tokens at high premiums to the extent that they will effectively get a cut of profits across almost all industries and contexts, globally.

>Especially with commodification and prices declining wouldn't that indicate there is more money to be made on the application-side of the models rather than the utility side

Don't forget that you're not looking at their expected steady-state for these companies. If you're willing to believe them at face-value, Sam Altman and Dario Amodei believe that they'll eventually create an AI more capable than the collection of all humans on Earth. That'd be a very valuable asset to own as a business. At that point, they may not even be in the business of selling tokens; they may become some version of a consulting company that everyone, from businesses to governments, effectively must use otherwise they'll be at a disadvantage compared to those who do use it. Pushed to the extreme, they may literally ascend past the point of just being a business and could usher in a new economic system in which they're the center of all activity.

Or maybe they just end up selling tokens indefinitely. Who knows. Regardless, if you're looking at these companies as they are now and trying to extrapolate "linearly," then you are failing to understand the intentions of such high-growth tech companies. It'd be like looking at Amazon back when they first started and not understanding that Jeff Bezos' had a lot more planned than just selling books online.

Management Consultants are usually accountants, not technology people who too often analyzing and providing a report and strategy and as much as possible except implementation let alone delivering the outcome. Junior labor is more profitable than senior labor. It's easier to hire someone for advisory, then consultants, who then get contractors to bang it out and by then who knows what got lost in translation. For a good while, I worked in rescuing these types of projects.

The model providers are often rooted from being researchers so they also have likely not spent much time in industry, let alone so many different industries. This is why we can see posts by leading AI folks who are sincerely amazed by how models are being used in industry.

That B2B experience + operations is on a different level because it exists in people's heads and not in the models.

text:
Title is a bit of an exaggeration but the question is more: if the frontier models are so good, why even sell them as your primary money maker?

Couldn't OpenAI or Anthropic make a lot more money by just starting companies themselves that leverage the models and building their own products?

Is selling tokens really the best strategy?

Especially with commodification and prices declining wouldn't that indicate there is more money to be made on the application-side of the models rather than the utility side
title: Ask HN: If the models are so good, why doesn't OpenAI just start 100 companies?
